name: PT Perusahaan Perkebunan London Sumatra Indonesia Tbk

frontmatter.title: London Sumatra — an estate the market barely pays for
frontmatter.summary: A mature planter whose cash is most of its market value, and whose estate the market barely pays for. We stay BUY at Rp4,722 (220.1%), charging the trapped-cash discount only to the September related-party balance and carrying the announced buyback in part. The reported DSI single export channel from 1 January 2027 is not yet a regulation and changes no direct input; palm sales are domestic and the only exports are rubber, cocoa and tea [S17, S20, S7].
thesis: Cash of IDR8,516.3bn and no interest-bearing debt at 30 September 2026 is most of the IDR10,264.0bn market capitalisation [S8, F37].
A mature estate earned 43.5% EBITDA margins at the deck price, with most output sold domestically to the parent at a persistent discount to the export benchmark [S7, S15].
The dividend is covered at a thirty per cent payout and a IDR750.0bn buyback is running; a probability-weighted part of the buyback is in the target and the dividend step-up is not [S12, S9].
The DCF, the config-blend multiples and book value all sit far above the price; the reverse DCF implies CPO near US$622/t [S0].
The risk is structural: related-party offtake, a controlling holder with no obligation to distribute, and a payout already cut once [S7, S12, S13].

blocks.text: **Revision, 9 November 2026.** This revision answers the red team and changes the model where the evidence did: the realisation is restated on one benchmark series, the trapped-cash discount is charged only to the related-party slice instead of the whole balance, the retained-cash bridge item that double-counted operating value is removed, the DCF is confirmed stub-aware from the September balance sheet, so no period-alignment item is needed, working capital returns to the last actual, the announced buyback is carried in part, and the bear now prices a domestic levy and a single-channel pass-through. Rating and method stand. The DHE SDA relaxation changes no input: palm and seed sales are domestic rupiah sales [S7, S17]. The price is Rp1,505 on 6 November 2026 [S0].

**The DSI export channel is reported, not yet regulated.** Press reports say that from 1 January 2027 coal, crude palm oil and ferro alloy must clear through PT Danantara Sumberdaya Indonesia's portal, which pre-checks price, quantity, quality, HS code and proceeds repatriation before customs [S20]. No regulation, presidential regulation or DSI decree is in our archive, so we label the regime unconfirmed, pending the implementing rule, and do not build it as a direct input. London Sumatra does not ship that way: oil-palm and seed sales were wholly domestic in both audited years, and the whole export line of IDR43.7bn against IDR5,511.7bn of revenue is rubber, cocoa and tea [S7, F49]. The channel reaches it only through the parent's refining netback and an unpublished fee [S21]; a one-to-five per cent pass-through into the related-party offtake is sized in the risk section and carried in the bear.

London Sumatra is a mid-sized Indonesian oil-palm estate owned by the Indofood group, priced as though the estate were a liability attached to a pile of cash. At Rp1,505 the company is worth about IDR10,264.0bn, against IDR8,516.3bn of cash and no interest-bearing debt at 30 September 2026 [S8]; the market pays barely more than the cash pile for the estate and mills.

That is not a distressed business. At the deck price the estate earned an EBITDA margin of 43.5%, a net profit of IDR1,887.8bn and Rp277 per share in the last audited year [S7], and the first nine months were better: net profit rose by two fifths [S3, S8].

Our target is Rp4,722, 220.1% above the price: a DCF at the through-cycle deck price plus cash with a probability-weighted governance discount on the related-party slice, corroborated by two multiples, with the related-party trapped-cash discount and the probability-weighted buyback as separate bridge items. The reverse DCF is the discipline: the price implies CPO of US$622/t at the reference year against a deck of 1,240.0 USD/t [S0, S15] — either the deck is wrong or the cash never reaches shareholders, and the implied price is below even the FY2023 trough.

PT Perusahaan Perkebunan London Sumatra Indonesia Tbk is one of Indonesia's oldest plantation companies, with nucleus estates in North Sumatra, South Sumatra, East Kalimantan, Java and Sulawesi [S6]. It sold 290.0 kt CPO of CPO from a nucleus planted area of just over one hundred and ten thousand hectares — about ninety-one thousand oil palm, sixteen thousand rubber and the balance cocoa and tea, with roughly seven per cent of the oil palm immature — and manages about thirty-five thousand hectares of plasma estates [S6].

The company reports three segments. Oil palm products, crude palm oil and palm kernel, are the overwhelming majority of revenue; SumBio seeds and a small rubber, cocoa and tea residual make up the rest [S7]. There is no refining of consequence: this is an upstream grower and miller, so its economics are the spread between the CPO price and the cost of a tonne.

More than three fifths of revenue is sold to PT Salim Ivomas Pratama, the listed subsidiary of Indofood Agri Resources that controls London Sumatra; including other related parties, almost two thirds moves within the group, and only a sliver is exported [S7]. Sales are market-referenced, and the audited realisation was stable in rupiah against the domestic Harga Referensi/KPB across the audited years, which suggests a structural domestic reference, not arbitrary transfer pricing; the 2026 dollar ratio is measured against a benchmark the World Bank replaced in January 2026, so it is not comparable with the audited years [S7, S15, F41]. Strategy is replanting, yield recovery and cost control: capex is a steady share of revenue, planted area has drifted down over five years, and there is no announced expansion or downstream project [S6].

The Salim family controls the company through Salim Ivomas and Indofood Agri Resources. PT Salim Ivomas Pratama holds 59.5% and Indofood Agri Resources a further small direct stake, so the group controls just under three fifths, and the public holds 40.4% [S13]. All 6,820 m shares are listed; no special-monitoring-board designation or notation letter appears in the filings and disclosures we hold [S7, S8]. The Yahoo insider field of seventy per cent is inconsistent with the company's own shareholder table and is not used. That ownership explains both the stable offtake and the persistent discount this report is about.

Indonesia is the world's largest CPO producer, and the price London Sumatra receives is set globally. The deck has CPO averaging 1,135.0 USD/t this year, rising next year and easing toward a long-run anchor of 1,150.0 USD/t in FY2029 money escalated with Indonesian inflation [S0, S15]. The near-term premium reflects tight balances and the expectation that El Nino will depress yields into next year; beyond that the deck assumes supply responds and the market settles toward marginal cost [S11].

Policy is active. Indonesia taxes CPO exports through a levy plus duty that moves monthly with a reference price; for November the combined charge fell by a fifth to 246.4 USD/t per tonne [S10]. The levy is borne by the exporter and matters here only at the margin because sales are domestic. The biodiesel mandate matters more: the move from a forty to a fifty per cent blend is the largest source of incremental domestic demand and underpins the government's willingness to keep export charges high [S10].

The live exchange-control change is separate and is not a palm-price policy. Under PP 21/2026, in force since June, non-oil-and-gas exporters must bring all DHE SDA onshore for at least twelve months, with conversion into rupiah capped at half; a fourth amendment to PP 36/2023 would lift that toward all of it, with implementing rules due by end-November [S17, S16]. It changes the currency in which the onshore balance may be held, not the dollars received or the duty to repatriate them, and its incidence here is negligible: palm and seed revenue is rupiah revenue from a domestic customer [S7]. Its one channel is the exchange rate — the sensitivity grid shows a two per cent move in the rupiah shifting the twelve-month value about two and a half per cent — which is second-order, so no input changes [S17, S0].

Export logistics are being centralised on top of that, on press reports we treat as unconfirmed until the implementing rule is issued. From 1 January 2027 coal, CPO and ferro alloy would file their declaration through DSI's customs-linked portal, which pre-checks price, quantity, quality, HS code and proceeds repatriation before the export service note issues [S20]. DSI calls itself a sole intermediary that will not disturb commercial negotiation or the movement of goods [S20]. GAPKI wants the role kept at intermediary rather than sole exporter that takes the producer's rights and risk, warning that an unclear scheme adds bureaucracy and cost on top of the export duty, levy, domestic-market obligation and DHE rules [S21]. No fee is published, so the incidence here is indirect — the parent's export netback and the price at which the group offtake can clear — and the report carries a sized pass-through in the bear.

The policy that would hit a wholly domestic seller directly is a domestic levy, a domestic-market obligation or a B50-funding charge on domestic CPO. No such charge is in force in November 2026: the levy and duty are export charges borne at shipment [S10]. But the B50 mandate we treat as demand support has a funding need, and the one policy that could meet it from a seller like London Sumatra is a charge on domestic sales. We therefore price a domestic levy of thirty to sixty dollars per tonne in the bear and state its target effect in the risk section, rather than assume domestic CPO is immune.

Competition is a cost-curve story: listed peers compete on yield, age profile and distance to mill, not brand. London Sumatra's estates are old, with a large mature base and a continuing replanting need; its cash cost of 7,791,431 rupiah per tonne rose because external FFB purchases climbed by more than a third [S7, S6]. It survives a trough on its balance sheet rather than its cost position. The moat is land and logistics — HGU rights, mills, plasma partnerships and the parent's refining system — real barriers that do not protect margins from a falling price [S6]. Five forces are unfavourable on the customer side, neutral on suppliers and favourable against new entrants [S6]. The variables that matter are the CPO price, the rupiah and the weather.

The data pack misstates the last audited year. Revenue rose 20.8% to IDR5,511.7bn on higher CPO volume and price and recovered palm kernel revenue; operating profit was IDR2,008.4bn and net profit to the parent IDR1,887.8bn [S7]. The pack's depreciation is unusable — a few billion rupiah against the audited IDR389.5bn — so we key the audited figure, lift FY2025 EBITDA to IDR2,397.8bn and the margin to 43.5%, restate FY2024 the same way, and strike every multiple off this base [S7, F12].

The cash cost is 7,791,431 rupiah per tonne, backed out of audited cost of sales after removing depreciation and allocating cost to the other lines; it rose because external FFB purchases climbed more than a third, and we hold it in real terms with inflation [S7]. Realisation is calibrated on the nine-month interim: CPO revenue over CPO volume gives a dollar price flat against the prior year while the benchmark rose, a ratio of 75.8% [S8, S3, S0]. The numerator and the denominator are on one series: the World Bank replaced its palm-oil series from January 2026, and the house deck records that pre-2026 annual averages and the 2026 monthly tape are not homogeneous [S15, S0]. The audited 858.1 USD/t against 1,007.0 USD/t is therefore not the like-for-like comparator; the domestic price series is the homogeneous one, and LSIP invoices against the Harga Referensi, averaging 14,234 rupiah per kilogram in the last audited year [S10, F41].

Revenue rises to IDR5,988.9bn this year, with EBITDA IDR2,684.3bn, net profit IDR2,189.5bn and Rp321 per share; the margin peaks with the deck and compresses as price eases and costs escalate. Volume is held at 300 kt because the estate is mature [S0, S7]. The calibration gate reads negative because it re-prices the old-series FY2025 benchmark with the new-series 2026 ratio: that is a definitional mismatch, not evidence that the estate earns less, and no published factor bridges the two series. On the comparison that is like-for-like, the model's dollar ASP of 860.3 USD/t at the current-year benchmark is flat against last year's realised 858.1 USD/t [S8, S3, S15].

Capex runs at 7.9% of revenue, working capital is the last actual's small share of revenue and most EBITDA becomes cash [S7]: IDR8,516.3bn at the third quarter against zero interest-bearing debt [S8]. The forecast holds operating working capital at the FY2025 ratio of revenue rather than the wider FY2024 spike; the working-capital caution sits in the bear, which stretches the ratio by three tenths [S0, F34]. The dividend is Rp83 at a thirty per cent payout and the buyback is a further return of capital [S12, S9]. Operating cash flow of IDR3,015.7bn exceeded net profit, so the accruals ratio is negative through the three years [S7, S0]. The flag is inventories, up to IDR830.8bn, a build of about a third against a tenth of revenue growth that one quarter explains but a second would not [S8, S3]. Biological-asset fair-value swings are non-cash, tax is below headline, and the opinion is unmodified [S7].

We use a DCF as the primary method, with EV/EBITDA and P/BV cross-checks at the industry weights of sixty, twenty-five and fifteen per cent — the method set for a price-taking grower whose value is the cash a mature asset earns over a cycle. Terminal growth is 2.5%, long-run rupiah inflation [S0].

The cost of equity is 11.2%: the rupiah ten-year yield of 7.4% [S18], a beta of 0.80 times the mature premium of 4.2% plus the country premium of 2.5%, net of the 1.6% sovereign default spread [S19]; with no net debt WACC equals it. The beta is the industry config default, not a measured regression — the house beta file holds a coal median only. It does not decide the rating: a beta a tenth above the default cuts the target about a twenty-fifth and one a quarter above about a fourteenth.

The DCF gives Rp5,078 per share, a terminal value of 45.8% of it, on an enterprise value of IDR24,692.1bn plus September net cash and the associate. The capitalised anchor is the deck's through-cycle 1,150.0 USD/t in FY2029 money escalated with inflation, so the first terminal year is 1,178.8 USD/t, not the 1,180.0 USD/t print [S0, S15]. The anchor is a fifth above the FY2023 to FY2025 average of 952.0 USD/t and a seventh above the last actual; the premium is disclosed and not added again. Running the DCF at the FY2023 to FY2025 average instead of the deck anchor cuts the DCF value to about seven eighths of the base, and at the current spot print it is close to the base; those are the two anchors the market can be asked to believe, and neither supports a price as low as today's.

The IDR1,261.1bn associate line in the bridge is not one entity. It is four equity-method holdings: Asian Assets Management Pte Ltd in Singapore, roughly a quarter held, carried at IDR760.3bn against net assets of IDR4,484.1bn; PT Aston Inti Makmur in Jakarta, roughly a quarter held, carried at IDR366.9bn against net assets of IDR3,775.6bn; and two smaller industrial-timber holdings [S7, S8, F62]. Both larger holdings are private, so there is no market price; their combined share of net assets is well above the carrying value, and the nine-month share of associate profit was IDR1.5bn, a negligible return on book [S8, F67]. The line is therefore an asset-value item, and book is a conservative mark, not an earnings multiple. Read against the market, cash at face plus the associate at book means the market pays about a fifth of one year's EBITDA for the estate, and about three tenths with the related-party haircut charged; excluding the associate entirely the estate is about four fifths of one year's EBITDA. The line is not counted twice: it is added once, in the bridge, and the estate multiple is shown both with and without it. The plasma receivables are a working-capital item inside other receivables, carried at expected recovery, and are not separately valued.

On asset value, the estate is 110,982 planted hectares, of which 84,744 are mature oil palm and the remainder rubber, cocoa and tea, with only a small immature oil-palm block [S6, F32, F40]. Net fixed assets of IDR5,087.6bn at 30 September over that planted area is a small number per hectare at historical cost, so book is not a replacement-cost mark; the DCF enterprise value over the same hectares is several times that, and the market's enterprise value of the same hectares is a fraction of both. We do not assign a cost-curve quartile: no public cost-curve dataset covering the Indonesian plantation names is in the archive, so we report the cash cost, the margin and the debt-free balance sheet that lets the estate survive a trough rather than claim a position we cannot source. The dividend anchor is the cross-check that matters: at 5.5% the dividend yield is below the cost of equity of 11.2%, so dividend capacity alone does not explain the value; the market is pricing a governance discount, not a yield. That is why we anchor on NAV and use the dividend and buyback as the return path.

The cross-checks do not use a config blend in the way the earlier draft said. EV/EBITDA comes from the engine's twenty-five-name peer median of 5.7x and gives Rp3,472; the own-history leg has too few clean observations because the pack's earlier EV/EBITDA years are distorted by impairment and near-zero EBITDA, so the blend falls back to the peer median [S0]. P/BV blends the peer median with an own average that is itself below book, to 1.1x, and gives Rp2,367. Both sit below the DCF — the EBITDA leg by about a third, the book leg by about a half. The peer set is wide and includes small caps on high multiples; at the narrower fifteen-name plantation median the EBITDA leg is roughly a fifth lower again, so the cross-check is weakest exactly where the red team tested it. The EBITDA leg is charged the full governance bridge against a metric that already holds the cash. If the estate never re-rates, the multiples are the better guide, and even they are far above the price.

The bridge now has two items, each disclosed separately from the operating value. First, the trapped-cash discount is charged only to the related-party cash at PT Bank Ina Perdana, IDR665.0bn at 30 September, 4.0% of assets and under a tenth of the cash balance, against a tenth of assets at the year-end [S8, F53, F54]. In the persistence state that slice is worth about two fifths of face; at even odds the charge is roughly three tenths of the related-party balance and a negligible share of total cash. Second, the announced IDR750.0bn buyback to 31 December 2026 [S9] is counted at half size and even odds, because it retires shares at a deep discount to intrinsic value but its size is a ceiling and its window short.

The other IDR7,629.3bn of third-party time deposits — at Danamon, OCBC NISP, Mega including the US dollar deposit, CIMB, SMBC, Mandiri, BRI and others — is carried at face [S8, F57]. There is no precedent or mechanism in our archive for a principal loss on deposits at unrelated banks, and the haircut is not a credit-loss assumption: it is the value of cash that is permanently undistributable to minorities. We apply it to the related-party slice where the group relationship is disclosed, and carry the whole-balance trap as the governance bear rather than as the base. Even odds stand on evidence both ways: the payout was cut from thirty-five to thirty per cent and there is no minority veto, but every year has been paid and a buyback is running [S12, S9, S13].

Charging the whole balance at even odds instead of only the related-party slice lowers the target by about a fifteenth; that is the variant the red team asked us to show, and it is not the base. With the whole balance trapped at certainty, the operating bear is worth about a third more than the current price — the governance-failure state no longer loses money, because the estate plus the face value of the cash covers the price. The price therefore implies something more extreme than the governance state: a CPO path below the FY2023 trough, as the reverse DCF shows. That state is quoted, not run: the bridge probability is one input shared by all scenarios [S12, S13].

The payout step-up to the sister's fifty per cent is not added to the value. Once the cash is credited at face, a higher payout distributes value already counted and is not an incremental asset; it matters only in the trapped state, which the bear carries. The buyback is the one capital-return lever that creates value for continuing holders, and it is in the bridge at a probability-weighted partial.

The price implies CPO of about US$622/t at the reference year — about half the deck's 1,240.0 USD/t and a third below the FY2023 to FY2025 average [S0, S15], below even the FY2023 trough. Alternatively, crediting cash at close to face and the associate at book, it implies about a fifth of one year's EBITDA for the estate. Either the market expects CPO below the cycle trough, or it expects the cash to be consumed by the group, or both. The dividend and the buyback are the only mechanisms that have returned value, and they are why we stay long.

The largest risk is the one we are implicitly betting against: that the discount is permanent. London Sumatra is a controlled subsidiary of a family group, most output is sold to its parent, and a material share of cash sits with a related bank — IDR665.0bn, 4.0% of total assets, withdrawable at the group's discretion [S8, F53]. Minority shareholders cannot force a distribution, the payout has been cut once, and a value investor can be right about the asset and wrong about the exit for years. That is the value-trap configuration, and we charge for it explicitly.

The second risk is CPO. The base uses the house deck, which embeds a near-term El Nino premium; if the weather fades and Malaysian stocks rebuild, price could fall by a quarter or more and the operating value with it [S11]. The bear models that with a volume shortfall, a working-capital stretch and a real cost base three tenths above the last actual. The third cluster is operational and regulatory. External FFB purchases are a flexible cost but a source of margin volatility; the levy and biodiesel mandate change the domestic price [S10]; and from January the reported single-channel export regime adds an unpublished intermediary cost between the group's refineries and the world market [S20, S21]. We size the channel: a one-to-five per cent pass-through into the related-party offtake, which is 63.3% of revenue, is about one and a half to eight per cent of EBITDA and moves the target by one to four per cent; it is carried in the bear's cost stress. The domestic levy is the policy that would hit a wholly domestic seller directly: at thirty to sixty dollars per tonne it would take seven to thirteen per cent of EBITDA and three to six per cent of the target, and the bear carries forty dollars inside its cost stress. A weaker rupiah helps the rupiah price but raises imported fertiliser and fuel costs. None is existential for a debt-free producer.

Two downsides are sized. FY2024 carried a IDR296.2bn impairment of the rubber plantations against a fixed-asset carrying amount of about five trillion rupiah, and the same assets could be written down again under the bear's conditions [S7]. The related-party cash, at IDR665.0bn, is a twenty-fifth of total assets and under a tenth of cash; a run on that relationship would remove a visible slice of liquidity in one step, and the base charges it at even odds.

Turnover of IDR17.6bn and a public float of 40.4% clear the fund's floor, so no liquidity discount applies; the constraint is ownership and willingness to distribute [S0, S13, F60]. We use the company's own shareholder table, not the Yahoo insider field, which is inconsistent with it.

The scenarios mirror the base shock for shock. The bear holds CPO at the FY2023 trough of 886.0 USD/t at the reference year [S15], with volume down about a sixth, the real cost base three tenths higher (including the domestic levy and the single-channel pass-through) and working capital stretched; it charges the related-party cash discount at even odds, so it is an operating bear rather than a governance state. It still produces Rp2,594, about seven tenths above the price: even at the cycle's realised low the market pays less than the estate alone is worth. With the whole balance trapped at certainty the same operating bear is about a third above the price, so the governance failure no longer loses money at the current price; what the price implies is more extreme than that, a CPO path below the FY2023 trough. The bull raises price by two fifths, volume about a sixth, releases working capital and holds costs a fifth below the last actual; the buyback is in the bridge and the payout step-up is not added. The probability-weighted target is Rp4,722. The signposts that would change our view are a sustained CPO break below the bear, a related-party transaction that transfers cash out below market value, another payout cut, a domestic levy materially above the bear's forty dollars, or the buyback being abandoned.

The controlling shareholder is PT Salim Ivomas Pratama, part of the Indofood Agri Resources group, holding 59.5%; Indofood Agri holds a small direct stake, so the group controls just under three fifths, and the public holds 40.4% of the 6,820 m shares [S13]. We use the company's own table, not the Yahoo insider field of seventy per cent, which adds up to an impossible total and is not used anywhere in this report [S0, S13]. We find no share-pledge disclosure, no control contest and no restatement, and the board comprises group nominees alongside independent commissioners [S7, S8].

Related-party dealings are the central governance fact. Sales of more than three fifths of revenue to the parent, FFB purchases from related estates, finance income on deposits at a related bank and group service companies all appear in the notes [S7]. Each is disclosed at market-referenced terms, and the audited realisation discount to the export benchmark was stable across the two audited years, the best available evidence that terms are not manipulated; the lower 2026 tape is treated as the domestic-reference effect [S7, S15]. It is still a structure in which the minority depends on the holder's goodwill, and the market prices that dependence.

The auditor is KAP Purwanto Susanti dan Surja, with an unmodified opinion and no change of auditor of note [S7]. The company does not revalue its plantations, so book value understates replacement cost, which is why P/BV is a floor rather than a target. The dividend record is the main counterweight: a payout every year, thirty per cent of profit for the last two years and thirty-five before [S12]. The cut is why the trap probability stays at even odds.

On ESG the exposures are land and deforestation, peat, labour and smallholder relations. The estates are long established, the company operates plasma partnerships, the industry's main social-licence mechanism, and reports against the national sustainability standard [S6]. Transition risk is low relative to social and regulatory risk.

The near-term catalyst is the full-year result and the dividend declaration that follows. The interim showed profit up two fifths and cash higher, so the base for the final dividend is strong [S3, S8].

The buyback runs to 31 December 2026 on internal cash [S9]; execution at the current price is accretive because the shares trade below the cash they represent. We treat completion as upside: the size is a ceiling and nothing commits the company to the full amount.

Third is policy: the B50 mandate and the monthly export levy reset determine the domestic CPO price and the group's offtake economics [S10], and a domestic levy or domestic-market obligation is the risk we watch for a wholly domestic seller. The implementing regulation for the DHE SDA conversion change is due by end-November, watched only for the exchange-rate channel [S17]. On 1 January the reported DSI portal is due to open for CPO and coal, unconfirmed until the implementing rule is issued; we watch the published intermediary fee and whether the group's export netback moves, the one route by which the regime can reach a wholly domestic seller [S20, S21].

The operational signposts are FFB output, extraction rate and external FFB purchases; the first nine months showed recovery on all three [S3], and a reversal would test the bear. The El Nino lag is the main reason to expect a weaker patch, which we would treat as an opportunity if the cash return continues. Above all we monitor related-party flows: a change in the offtake, the deposit relationship or the group's willingness to let cash accumulate matters more than the CPO price [S7, S13].

bear.narrative: The discount persists and the cycle troughs at the same time. The related-party cash slice at Bank Ina Perdana of Rp665.016bn at 30-Sep-2026 is not withdrawn and the whole-balance governance failure is quoted as a separate state in section 5 [S8, F53]. On top of that, CPO is held at 71.5% of the deck for the whole forecast, which is USD 886/t at the FY2027E reference year - the FY2023 trough of the World Bank Pink Sheet series [S15] - and about USD 812/t in the current year, well below the FY2023-25 realised average of USD 952/t and the deck anchor [S0]. The El Nino premium unwinds and Malaysian stocks rebuild [S11], a weaker FFB crop cuts volume 15% from the 300 kt plan, and the parent receivable stretches working capital 30% [F34]. The cost stress is 30% above the FY2025 real level: 20% from external FFB and fertiliser, plus a USD40/t domestic CPO levy and a 2% pass-through of the DSI single-channel fee into the parent offtake, together about 8% of the cash cost. The domestic levy is the one policy that reaches a wholly domestic seller if the B50 funding need is met from domestic CPO; it is a bear risk, not a base assumption, because no domestic levy is in force in November 2026 [S10]. With the whole balance trapped at certainty instead of even odds this operating bear is worth Rp1,926, still above the current price: that is the governance-failure state, and it is quoted in section 5 rather than run as a fourth scenario because the bridge probability is a single model input shared by all scenarios.

bull.narrative: A severe El Nino and the B50 mandate lift CPO two fifths above the deck, as they did in the 2021-22 squeeze [S10, S11]; a normal Q4, the maturing 6,054 ha of immature oil palm and a yield recovery from the weather-depressed base take volume 17.6% above the 300 kt plan; faster collection from SIMP releases working capital; and the extraction-rate and FFB-purchase programme hold the real cash cost a fifth below the FY2025 level [S3]. The announced Rp750bn buyback, running 26-Oct to 31-Dec-2026 on internal cash [S9], is carried as a probability-weighted partial in the valuation bridge, not as a scenario shock because its size is a ceiling. A step-up to the group sister's 50% payout is a board decision and is not added to the value: once the cash is credited at face, a higher payout distributes value already counted and is not an incremental asset; it matters only in the trapped state that the bear carries.

sensitivity.title: 12-month value vs benchmark price and IDR/USD
12-month value vs volume and unit cost intensity

OPS.label: Cash cost + royalty per unit (price currency)

assumptions.label: Sales volume plan
assumptions.basis: FY2026E is the 9M-2026 run-rate plus a normal Q4: CPO sales were 222 kt in the nine months (+7% yoy, [S3]) and Q4-2025 was 82.5 kt of the 290 kt year [F1], giving about 300 kt. Production supports it: 9M-2026 CPO output rose 12% to 227 kt on nucleus FFB up 7% to 850 kt [S3], and FY2025 production was 292 kt [F33]. The estate is mature and not expanding: nucleus oil palm is 90,798 ha with only 7% immature [F32], so the plan is held flat at 300 kt with no yield-growth assumption, inside the 15% drift gate. FY2025 sales of 290 kt are the last audited actual [F1].

assumptions.label: Realised price / benchmark
assumptions.basis: Recalibrated on the last actual, the 9M-2026 interim, and held flat. CPO (MKS) revenue of Rp3,342.357bn [S8, F48] over 222 kt of CPO sales [S3, F47] is Rp15.056m per tonne; at the model's FY2026E usd_idr of 17,570 [S0] that is USD 856.9/t against the deck's 9M-2026 average of USD 1,131/t (Q1 1,081, Q2 1,164, Q3 1,148, [S15]), a realisation of 0.758. The numerator and the denominator are on one series: the World Bank Pink Sheet states "October 2026: Replacement series for Palm oil from January 2026" [S15, p.3], and the house deck records that "the World Bank re-based the palm oil series from January 2026 ... so pre-2026 annual averages and the 2026 monthly tape are not perfectly homogeneous" [fund record]. The audited FY2025 ratio of 0.852 (Rp14.114m/t against the pre-replacement 1,007 series at 16,448.09 [F3]) is therefore not the like-for-like comparator and is not used: no published factor bridges the old and new series, and applying a 2026-series ratio to a 2025-series benchmark is the mismatch the red team identified. What is homogeneous in rupiah is the realised price against the domestic Harga Referensi/KPB: Rp14.114m/t in FY2025 against the Rp14,234/kg KPB average [F41, S6], or 0.992. The 9M-2026 realised rupiah price of Rp15.056m/t is +6.7% on FY2025 while the new-series dollar benchmark is +12.3%, and the rupiah is +6.8% weaker, so the company takes the domestic reference rather than the export print; that domestic-reference lag and the unquantified series break together explain why the model carries 0.758 and not 0.852. Holding 0.758 flat rather than fading it is the last-actual rule; the peer ratios near 0.78 are measured against other benchmarks and are not directly comparable. At the 30-Sep-2026 balance-sheet rate of Rp17,998 [S8] the same revenue/volume is USD 836.5/t, a 0.740 ratio, which brackets the estimate from below.

assumptions.label: Share of volume under a price cap (e.g. DMO)
assumptions.basis: Zero: no DMO-style domestic price cap applies to Indonesian CPO sales in this period; the B40/B50 mandate is a demand driver, not a cap on LSIP's selling price [S10].

assumptions.label: Strip ratio (bcm per tonne) or cost-intensity factor
assumptions.basis: Palm oil cost intensity is expressed per tonne of CPO, so the intensity factor is 1.0 and all cash cost sits in cost_per_bcm; there is no overburden analogue in a plantation [S7].

assumptions.label: Cash cost per tonne of CPO (reporting currency)
assumptions.basis: Anchored on the last audited year and escalated with IDR inflation only. FY2025 COGS of Rp3,250.368bn [F7] less the Rp373.058bn of depreciation inside it [F30] leaves Rp2,877.310bn of cash cost for all products; the non-CPO cost of Rp617.854bn on Rp1,418.588bn of PK, rubber and other revenue at the 56.45% other margin [F28] is stripped out, leaving Rp2,259.456bn of CPO cash cost, or Rp7.791m per tonne on 290 kt [F1]. That is 21% above FY2024's Rp6.420m [F31] because external FFB purchases jumped to Rp672.332bn from Rp488.924bn [S7]; we hold the FY2025 level rather than extrapolate either year. The 2.5% annual escalation is the macro deck's long-run IDR inflation [S0], so the real cost base is flat and the FY2025 gross-margin gain is not assumed to repeat.

assumptions.label: Fuel share of mining cost
assumptions.basis: Engine default scalar set to zero: the fuel driver is empty for PLANTATIONS, so the fuel term does not enter the cost build [S7].

assumptions.label: Other cash cost per unit (haul, barge, process)
assumptions.basis: Zero: haulage, milling and port costs are already inside the per-tonne CPO cash cost backed out of the FY2025 LK [F30]; a separate unit line would double count.

assumptions.label: Royalty rate (flat regimes)
assumptions.basis: Zero: 63.26% of revenue is sold domestically to SIMP [F34] and Indonesia's CPO export levy is borne by the exporter at shipment (USD 246.36/t, [F38]), not by LSIP on a domestic sale. The FY2025 cost-of-sales note carries no royalty or export-levy line [S7].

assumptions.label: Other revenue (PK, rubber, others)
assumptions.basis: FY2025 non-CPO revenue was Rp1,418.588bn: palm kernel and related products 1,093.304, rubber 149.982 and others 175.302 [F28]. It is escalated at 2.5% IDR inflation with flat volume, since PK output tracks CPO throughput and rubber prices move with the same cost base [S7, S0]; the FY2024 comparative of Rp921.664bn [F29] was lower because PK prices were weak, not because the product mix changed.

assumptions.label: Gross margin on other revenue
assumptions.basis: 56.45%: the FY2025 residual implies Rp617.854bn of cost on Rp1,418.588bn of non-CPO revenue once the CPO cash cost is set at Rp7.791m per tonne [F28]. PK and rubber are by-products of FFB already harvested for CPO, so the incremental cost is pressing, handling and freight only; the ratio is held flat.

assumptions.label: D&A per unit (reporting currency)
assumptions.basis: FY2025 total D&A of Rp389.453bn (fixed assets 383.284, right-of-use 5.129, deferred charges 1.040, [F13]) over the 300 kt plan is Rp1.298m per tonne. The pack's Rp4.8bn D&A line is defective and has been replaced by the audited Note 25 charge [F13]. The 9M-2026 charge of Rp304.770bn (segment 292.398 plus unallocated 12.372, [S8]) annualises to about Rp406bn, so the FY2025 base is not stale. Escalated at 2.5% IDR; there is no revaluation uplift because LSIP does not apply the PSAK 16 revaluation model [S6].

assumptions.label: Sustaining capex per unit (reporting currency)
assumptions.basis: FY2025 additions to fixed assets were Rp433.312bn [F15], or 7.9% of revenue, spread across replanting, machinery, plasma and infrastructure (segment capex 393.856 plus unallocated 39.456, [S7]); over the 300 kt plan that is Rp1.444m per tonne. The 9M-2026 run-rate of Rp264.471bn [S8] supports the same intensity. Held in real terms with 2.5% IDR escalation rather than assuming a step-down after the current replanting push [S0].

assumptions.label: Other capex (expansion projects)
assumptions.basis: Zero: LSIP's capex is volume-linked replanting, machinery and plasma support rather than discrete expansion projects, and the planted area has been flat-to-down (110,982 ha in 2025 vs 114,111 ha in 2021, [F32]); all of it is carried in capex_unit.

assumptions.label: Operating working capital / revenue
assumptions.basis: 3.3%, the FY2025 actual: operating working capital was Rp181.720bn or 3.3% of revenue in FY2025 [S0]. The FY2024 spike of 21.7% and FY2023's 7.3% [S0] are not extrapolated: the swing is the receivable from parent SIMP, 63.26% of revenue [F34], and the last actual is the right anchor. The working-capital caution is carried in the bear, which stretches the ratio 30%.

assumptions.label: Effective tax rate
assumptions.basis: 17.2%, the FY2025 effective rate: income tax of Rp391.187bn [F24] on pre-tax profit of Rp2,277.542bn [F9]. Held flat; the 22% headline is reduced by the permanent differences on plasma and land income that recur in the LK [S7].

assumptions.label: Cost of debt (on opening debt)
assumptions.basis: 8% on a negligible balance: FY2025 finance costs were Rp1.176bn [F23] against lease liabilities of under Rp1bn, and the group carries no bank borrowings at 30-Sep-2026 [F37]. The rate is set so a future lease or drawdown prices sensibly rather than at the engine's 15% clamp.

assumptions.label: Yield on opening cash
assumptions.basis: 4.6%, the three-year average of finance income over opening cash: 5.06% in FY2025 (Rp276.021bn [F21] on Rp5,453.691bn), 4.81% in FY2024 and 4.04% in FY2023 [S0]. The balance is held largely on deposit and partly at related-party Bank Ina Perdana, which supplied Rp44.005bn of FY2025 finance income [S7].

assumptions.label: Net new borrowing
assumptions.basis: Zero: the group has no interest-bearing bank debt at 30-Sep-2026, only lease liabilities [F37, S8], and capex plus the dividend are covered by operating cash flow of Rp3,015.733bn in FY2025 [S7]. The announced Rp750bn buyback [S9] is assumed to be funded from cash, not debt.

assumptions.label: Other non-operating items
assumptions.basis: Zero: no recurring non-operating income or charge is disclosed beyond the associate line (a Rp5.691bn loss in FY2025) and that is immaterial against EBITDA [S7].

assumptions.label: Minorities' share of net profit
assumptions.basis: Zero: non-controlling interests are Rp3.833bn of a Rp13,999.946bn equity base and their share of profit was a Rp1.401bn loss in FY2025 [S7], so the minority line is immaterial.

assumptions.label: Dividend payout
assumptions.basis: 30%: the company declares 30% of profit, DPS Rp83 for FY2025 and Rp65 for FY2024 on 6,819,963,965 shares [F18, S12]. The FY2025 cash payment of Rp443.234bn was the FY2024 dividend [F17]; the 30% policy is held rather than the engine's default.

assumptions.label: Change in share count
assumptions.basis: Zero: shares outstanding are 6,819,963,965 and unchanged across the audited years [F20]. The Rp750bn buyback announced in October 2026 [S9] is not yet executed and its size is a ceiling, so it is treated as upside in section 5 rather than modelled as a completed reduction.

assumptions.label: Terminal growth (DCF)
assumptions.basis: 2.5% nominal IDR, the macro deck's long-run inflation [S0]. With volume flat and CPO prices and costs both escalating at about inflation, real FCFF is flat; a 4% terminal rate would add real growth the business has not shown (nucleus FFB has been flat at 1.34-1.38m tonnes since 2021, [S6]).

assumptions.label: SG&A / revenue (cash)
assumptions.basis: 4.6%, the FY2025 net operating cost ratio implied by the filing: gross profit Rp2,261.338bn less operating profit Rp2,008.388bn = Rp252.950bn of net operating cost on Rp5,511.706bn of revenue [F11]. It nets other operating income (Rp136.905bn of FX, land-usage and PK-shell income) against selling (Rp73.099bn) and G&A (Rp247.878bn) and the Rp59.571bn bio-asset fair-value loss [S7]. FY2024's 9.7% is not the run-rate because it carries the Rp296.164bn one-off impairment [F12]. Held flat, so no drift.

challenges.challenge: The calibration.ebitda BLOCK is answered with the sentence that S15 carries no series-replacement note for palm oil and the earlier re-base claim is withdrawn, but S15 page 3 states October 2026: Replacement series for Palm oil from January 2026, and the house deck basis in fund record says the World Bank re-based the palm oil series from January 2026 so pre-2026 annual averages and the 2026 monthly tape are not perfectly homogeneous. The 0.758 realisation divides a 2026 rupiah price by a re-based 2026 dollar benchmark, then the calibration test applies that ratio to the pre-2026 FY2025 benchmark of 1,007; the domestic-reference-lag-not-a-series-break explanation in section 3 is therefore unsupported. This reverses the prior round C23, which was wrong on the source.
challenges.answer: Accepted; the prior round was wrong on the source. The realisation basis now quotes S15 p.3 verbatim ("October 2026: Replacement series for Palm oil from January 2026") and the fund record basis ("the World Bank re-based the palm oil series from January 2026 ... so pre-2026 annual averages and the 2026 monthly tape are not perfectly homogeneous"). 0.758 is fitted wholly inside the 2026 new series: 9M-2026 CPO revenue Rp3,342.357bn / 222 kt = Rp15.056m/t = USD856.9/t at 17,570, against the new-series 9M-2026 average of USD1,131/t [S8, S3, S15]. The audited 0.852 divides a rupiah price by the pre-replacement 1,007 series and is therefore not the like-for-like comparator; no published factor bridges the two series. The calibration.ebitda justification is restated as a series break in the denominator plus a domestic-reference lag in the numerator (the rupiah/KPB ratio is 0.992 [F41]), and the gate is disclosed as not like-for-like. For completeness the engine target at 0.780 is Rp4,849 and at 0.852 is Rp5,268 [S15].

challenges.challenge: Realisation 0.758 is the model dominant driver (about 2.3% of the DCF per percentage point; returning to the audited 0.852 adds roughly 30%), yet it is set 11pp below the last audited ratio, below every plantation peer with a domestic book (SIMP 0.780, TAPG 0.775, PGUN 0.790, AALI 0.879, ANJT 0.865) and supported by a nine-month ratio whose denominator is on a different series. Its own basis records 0.740 at the 30-Sep spot rate, so the input is not stable.
challenges.answer: Accepted on mechanism and instability. A monthly company realised-price series is not published, so the basis uses the finest available cuts: 9M-2026 realised Rp15.056m/t against the quarterly new-series benchmark (Q1 1,081, Q2 1,164, Q3 1,148) [S8, S3, S15], and FY2025 Rp14.114m/t against the Rp14,234/kg Harga Referensi/KPB average, 0.992 in rupiah [F41, S6]. The mechanism that widens the dollar discount is the domestic reference: in 9M-2026 the realised rupiah price rose 6.7% while the new-series dollar benchmark rose 12.3% and the rupiah weakened 6.8%, so the company tracks the domestic reference, not the export print. At the 30-Sep-2026 rate of Rp17,998 the same revenue/volume is 0.740, which brackets the estimate from below. Targets: 0.780 gives Rp4,849, 0.852 gives Rp5,268, versus the Rp4,721 base [S15, S8].

challenges.challenge: A 58.9% haircut at 50% probability is applied to the whole Rp8,516.3bn cash balance, of which Rp7,629.3bn (90%) is term deposits at unrelated banks (Danamon 3,078.5, OCBC NISP 1,500.0, Mega 685.0, CIMB 300.0, SMBC 200.0, BRI 80.0, Mandiri 94.0); the related-party slice is Rp665.0bn, 7.8% of cash. The only evidence given is a payout cut from 35% to 30% and the absence of a minority veto. No precedent or mechanism is cited for a principal loss on deposits at seven unrelated banks.
challenges.answer: Accepted. The 58.9% haircut is now charged only to the Rp665.016bn related-party cash at Bank Ina Perdana, 7.8% of the cash balance and under a tenth of cash (F53) [S8]. The Rp7,629.3bn of third-party balances and time deposits at Danamon, OCBC NISP, Mega, CIMB, SMBC, Mandiri and BRI is carried at face because no precedent or mechanism for principal loss on unrelated-bank deposits exists in the archive [S8, F57]. The persistence slice is worth about two fifths of face, so at even odds the charge is Rp195.85bn. Charging the whole balance at even odds instead would lower the target to Rp4,401 from Rp4,721 (about a fifteenth), and the whole-balance trap is carried as the governance bear (target Rp1,926 at certainty), not the base [S12, S9].

challenges.challenge: The second bridge item treats EV less PV of dividends (24,513.3 less 9,473.3 = Rp15,040.1bn) as trapped cash and haircuts it 58.9% x 0.5. That residual is the PV of FCFF the terminal value assumes is reinvested in the estate to sustain the going concern; the arithmetic depends only on the dividend schedule and on no cash-balance data, and the model own net-debt line reaches -Rp27,466.5bn by FY2035.
challenges.answer: Accepted; the item was a category error and is removed. The EV-less-PV-of-dividends residual is the PV of FCFF the terminal value assumes is reinvested in the estate to sustain the going concern; it is operating value, not a cash balance, and its arithmetic depends only on the dividend schedule. The bridge now charges trapped cash only on the related-party cash balance at the same 30-Sep-2026 date as the engine net debt, separately from operating PV; the operating DCF is untouched. The bridge is now two disclosed items (related-party trapped cash, buyback) [S8, S7].

challenges.challenge: The DCF credits FY2026E FCFF of Rp1,558.9bn in full while the bridge uses the 30-Sep-2026 cash of Rp8,516.3bn. The post_bs_review asserts the opposite (the engine discounts the full FY2026E FCFF at time zero so the July-September cash generation is already inside that flow), but the September balance already contains the January-September generation, so about 9/12 of FY2026E FCFF (about Rp1,170bn, about Rp170 per share) is counted twice.
challenges.answer: Rebutted on the mechanics, with the model checked. The engine DCF is stub-aware from the 2026-09-30 balance-sheet date: the FY2026E row counts only 1 October to 31 December (fraction 0.251882 of FY2026E FCFF, PV Rp462.7bn at the 2026-11-09 as-of date), so January-September generation inside the September cash is not counted twice. The earlier post_bs_review assertion that the engine discounts FY2026E in full at time zero was wrong; it has been corrected, and the period-alignment bridge item I had added in response to this challenge has been removed because it was itself a double correction. Target effect of the removal: Rp4,559 to Rp4,721 (+Rp162 per share). The DCF/bridge dates are now consistent [S8].

challenges.challenge: The 46% terminal value capitalises a USD1,150/t anchor that the deck own basis builds from the September-2026 spot print (1,180) plus a biodiesel premium; it is not the 10-year real average or long-run incentive price the commodity card requires. The anchor is 21% above the FY2023-25 average (952) and 14% above the last actual (1,007), and the FY2027E 1,240 is 6.5% above the highest number printed in the cited pink-sheet row (1,164).
challenges.answer: Accepted, with the anchor disclosed. The base DCF capitalises the deck through-cycle anchor of USD1,150/t in FY2029 money, which is a fifth above the FY2023-FY2025 average of 952 and a seventh above the FY2025 actual of 1,007 [S15]. Running the same model at 952 gives a target of Rp4,132 (still 175% above the price), at 1,180 gives Rp4,810, versus the Rp4,721 base. The report states that the market is using neither: the reverse DCF implies USD622/t at the reference year, half the deck and below the FY2023 trough, i.e. a governance/terminal discount rather than a lower price anchor [S0, S15].

challenges.challenge: The bridge adds Rp1,261.1bn of associates at book, 12.3% of the Rp10,264bn market cap and about 8% of the DCF value, without naming the entity, giving its earnings, or stating why book is realisable. S8 shows 9M-2026 share of associate profit of Rp1.532bn, a 0.1% return on that carrying value. Section 4 then uses the same Rp1,261bn to claim the estate trades at 1.25x EBITDA, so the number is load-bearing twice.
challenges.answer: Accepted. The associates are named: Asian Assets Management Pte Ltd (24.98%, net assets Rp4,484.144bn, FY2025 profit Rp18.466bn) carried at Rp760.257bn, and PT Aston Inti Makmur (24.99%, net assets Rp3,775.619bn, FY2025 profit Rp44.842bn) carried at Rp366.946bn, plus two smaller industrial-timber holdings [S7, S8, F62-F66]. Both larger holdings are private, so no market price exists; each is carried below the group's share of net assets, so book is conservative. The 9M share of associate profit is Rp1.532bn, a 0.1% return on book (F67), so the line is an asset-value item. Estate multiples at the market price: about 0.20x FY2025 EBITDA with cash at face and the associate at book, 0.29x with the related-party haircut, 0.81x with the associate excluded.

challenges.challenge: DSI is concluded nil because LSIP own palm exports are zero, correct on the segment note, but 63.26% of revenue is sold to SIMP, the parent whose refinery and export netback the single-channel regime directly changes, and the report itself says the channel reaches LSIP through the parent refining netback and an unpublished fee. That channel is asserted at zero and never sized in any scenario from 1-Jan-2027, the first forecast year.
challenges.answer: Accepted. The channel is sized: a 1-5% pass-through into the related-party offtake (63.26% of revenue) is Rp38-189bn of EBITDA, one and a half to eight per cent, and moves the target from Rp4,721 to Rp4,685 at 1% and Rp4,543 at 5% (0.8% to 3.8%). It is carried inside the bear's cost stress (2% pass-through) and the report now states the target range in the risk section [S8, S20, S21]. We cannot source that the parent is unable to pass the fee through, so we do not claim it.

challenges.challenge: The report dismisses export levies because LSIP sales are domestic, but never considers a domestic levy, DMO or B50-funding charge on domestic CPO, the one policy that would hit a 100%-domestic seller directly. The B50 mandate is cited as demand support while its funding need is treated as a reason to keep export charges high, not as a reason to levy domestic sales.
challenges.answer: Accepted. A domestic levy of USD30/t costs Rp148 per share (target Rp4,573, -3.1%) and USD60/t costs Rp297 (target Rp4,424, -6.3%); that is seven to thirteen per cent of FY2025 EBITDA. The bear carries USD40/t inside its 30% cost stress, and the report now gives the domestic-levy target range alongside the exit-levy discussion [S10]. We found no source making domestic CPO immune; the base simply assumes no domestic levy is in force in November 2026, and the signpost is a levy materially above the bear's forty dollars.

challenges.challenge: The report calls the payout step-up and buyback the route to value and quantifies them at about Rp258 and Rp206 per share (roughly 12% of the target), but excludes both from base and bull; the bull is only a price/volume case. A net-cash company buying 7.3% of its shares at 0.5x book and 0.51x EV/EBITDA is the most likely mechanism to close the discount, not a tail.
challenges.answer: Accepted in part. The buyback is now in the base bridge at half size and even odds (Rp351.3bn expected), worth about Rp22 per share in the probability-weighted target, with the full-programme intrinsic value at about Rp206 per share [S9, F58]. The payout step-up to 50% is not added, and the reason is arithmetic, not caution: once the September cash is credited at face, a higher payout distributes value already counted and adds nothing; it matters only in the trapped state, which the bear carries. The new expected value is Rp4,721 (bull Rp6,991, bear Rp2,594) [S9, S12].

challenges.challenge: No asset-value work: 110,982 ha planted (84,744 ha mature) is carried at Rp5,088bn of fixed assets, and the report says P/BV is a floor without valuing the land, the tree-age profile, the cost-curve quartile or the dividend-capacity yield against NAV, all explicit items in the commodity card output contract. The associate and the Rp112.2bn plasma receivables are likewise unvalued.
challenges.answer: Accepted on the asset work, with one limit stated. Planted area is 110,982 ha, of which 84,744 ha mature oil palm and a small immature block (6,054 ha, down from 8,223 ha five years earlier) [S6, F32, F40]. Sourced per-hectare marks: net fixed assets Rp45.8m per planted hectare at historical cost (F61/F32), DCF enterprise value about Rp222m per hectare, and the market's enterprise value about Rp16m per hectare. The dividend-capacity yield is 5.5% against an 11.18% cost of equity, so yield alone does not carry the value. No public cost-curve dataset covering these names is in the archive, so we do not assign a quartile and say so. The Rp112.2bn plasma receivables are inside other receivables at expected recovery (about 2% of assets) and are not separately valued [S7, S8].

challenges.challenge: Section 6 says insider ownership near 70.0% overlaps with the group holdings [S0, S13], but S13 shows SIMP 59.51%, Indofood Agri 0.11%, one director 212,000 shares and public 40.38%; 70% plus 40.38% is impossible. The liquidity floor and the no-liquidity-discount conclusion rest on the same float.
challenges.answer: Accepted. Ownership is restated to S13: SIMP 59.51% plus Indofood Agri Resources 0.11%, so the group controls 59.62%, and the public holds 40.38% at 30-Sep-2026 (40.40% at 31-Dec-2025), each holder below 5% [S13, F59, F60]. The Yahoo insider field of 70% is impossible against that table (70% plus 40.38% exceeds 100%), is deleted from the report and is not used for the liquidity test; the float and turnover clear the floor on the company's own table.

challenges.challenge: The entire DSI update rests on two same-day news items (CNBC Indonesia and KaltengPos, both 9 Nov 2026); no regulation, presidential regulation or DSI decree is in the archive, yet the report states the regime as settled (resmi, must file). The materiality conclusion of no input changes inherits that uncertainty, and the cited DSI detail (pre-clearance on price/quantity/quality/HS/repatriation) is accurate to S20.
